topics.title: Functions and Use of Digital Devices, and Notation

items.definition: General-purpose computers for one person: desktops and laptops.
items.examples: A designer's desktop; a student's laptop.
items.examTip: Desktop: more power for the price, upgradeable. Laptop: portable, battery, less upgradeable.
keyFacts: Key parts are the CPU, RAM, storage and GPU, and their specification decides how fast tasks run
Run a full OS (Windows, macOS, Linux), so they can run almost any software the user needs
Used for office work, gaming and creative work, because they have the power and screen space for long tasks

items.definition: One device that combines printing, scanning, copying and sometimes fax.
items.examples: An office printer/scanner/copier.
items.examTip: Saves space and money, but if it breaks, every function is lost.
keyFacts: Cheaper than separate machines, and take up less space in the office
Single point of failure: if it breaks, printing, scanning and copying all stop at once
Often networked, so staff can scan straight to email or a shared folder

items.definition: Portable battery-powered devices with a touchscreen and mobile OS, e.g. phones and tablets.
items.examples: iPhone; iPad; Apple Watch.
items.examTip: Always connected, but smaller screens, limited battery and easily lost.
keyFacts: Connect by Wi-Fi and 4G/5G, so users stay online away from home or the office
Touch interface running iOS or Android, so they are easy to use without a keyboard or mouse
Sensors (GPS, camera, NFC) enable maps, photos and contactless payments
Apps come from app stores, which check them, so users are less likely to install malware

items.definition: Powerful computers that provide files, apps or web pages to other computers on a network.
items.examples: A file server for shared documents; a web server hosting a website.
items.examTip: Know the three: file (stores files), application (runs software), web (serves pages).
keyFacts: File server gives central shared storage, so staff work from one copy and backups are easier
Application server runs apps for clients, so software is managed and updated in one place
Web server delivers pages over HTTP/HTTPS, so users anywhere can reach the organisation's website
Built to run 24/7, with features like spare power supplies, so services stay available

comparisonTable.title: Server Types Compared
rows: Stores and manages access to shared files/folders
Company shared drive (H: drive in Windows domain)
Hosts and runs software applications for network clients
Internal clients running client-side of the application
ERP system, database server, email server (Exchange)
Hosts website files, handles HTTP/HTTPS requests from browsers
Apache/Nginx hosting company website; IIS hosting intranet

items.definition: Devices mainly for leisure, e.g. games consoles, smart TVs and streaming sticks.
items.examples: PlayStation 5; a smart TV; Fire TV Stick.
items.examTip: Now internet-connected: link to streaming and online entertainment.
keyFacts: Consoles offer online multiplayer, so friends can play together from different homes
Smart TVs run streaming apps, so users watch on demand without extra boxes
Connected devices raise privacy concerns, because they can collect viewing habits and voice data

items.definition: Devices that capture photos or video digitally.
items.examples: DSLR; GoPro; CCTV; phone camera.
items.examTip: High-resolution photos and video need lots of storage and bandwidth.
keyFacts: More megapixels gives better quality but bigger files, so more storage is needed
4K video needs large storage, so users need big memory cards or cloud space
CCTV records continuously, so it needs a lot of storage and footage is often overwritten after a set time

items.definition: Devices or apps that use GPS satellites to find your location and plan routes.
items.examples: A sat nav; Google Maps; tracking delivery vans.
items.examTip: GPS gives position; live traffic needs an internet connection.
keyFacts: GPS works without mobile data, because it uses satellite signals, so it works in remote areas
Phone apps add live traffic, so routes avoid jams and journeys are quicker
Fleet tracking for deliveries, so companies know where vehicles are and can give accurate arrival times
Location data is personal data under GDPR, so it must be collected with consent and kept secure

items.definition: Hardware for sending and receiving information, e.g. phones, routers and modems.
items.examples: Mobile phones; VoIP phones; routers.
items.examTip: The hardware layer of networks: link to Section B.
keyFacts: Modem converts signals for phone or cable lines, so digital data can travel over them
Router connects the LAN to the internet, sending data between the two networks
VoIP phones make calls over the internet, which is cheaper than traditional phone lines

items.term: Embedded Systems (Sensors and Internet of Things)
items.definition: A computer built into a device to do one job; IoT devices are embedded systems connected to the internet.
items.examples: A washing machine controller; a smart thermostat; a smart meter.
items.examTip: Embedded = one fixed job. IoT = embedded + internet. IoT security is often weak.
keyFacts: Single purpose with little or no interface, so they are cheap, reliable and use little power
IoT devices send data to the cloud, so they can be monitored and controlled remotely
Weak default passwords and rare updates make them easy to hack, e.g. to recruit them into a botnet

subtopics.title: Function and Use of Digital Devices by Context

items.definition: Using devices for everyday tasks: communication, entertainment, shopping and banking.
items.examTip: Consider privacy when discussing personal use.
keyFacts: Phones for messaging, maps and media, so people stay connected and entertained on the move
Laptops for shopping and banking, because a bigger screen makes forms and comparisons easier
Smart speakers and thermostats at home, so devices can be controlled by voice or remotely

items.term: Education and Training Use of Digital Devices
items.definition: Using devices to support teaching, learning and assessment.
items.examTip: Link to online education and the digital divide.
keyFacts: Interactive whiteboards let teachers show and annotate content, so lessons are more engaging
Laptops and tablets for research, so learners can find information and work independently
VLEs such as Google Classroom hold work and feedback, so learners can access them from home

items.definition: Using devices to communicate and interact with others online.
items.examTip: Give both sides: connection and support vs cyberbullying and addiction.
keyFacts: Social media and messaging apps let people stay in touch, wherever friends and family are
Online gaming communities connect people with shared interests across the world
Risks include cyberbullying, loss of privacy and addiction, which can harm wellbeing

items.definition: Using devices to support buying, selling and managing stock.
items.examTip: Link to online retail and stock control.
keyFacts: EPOS tills update stock automatically, so shops know when to reorder
Barcode and RFID scanners read product details quickly, so checkout and stocktaking are faster and accurate
Self-checkouts cut staff costs, because one worker can supervise several tills
Contactless card readers make payments faster, so queues move quicker

items.definition: Using computer-controlled machines, robots and sensors to automate manufacturing.
items.examTip: Key themes: CNC machines, robots, sensors for quality control.
keyFacts: CNC machines cut parts precisely, so every part is identical and waste is reduced
Robots assemble, weld and paint, so production runs faster and staff avoid dangerous jobs
Sensors monitor machines in real time, so faults are spotted before they cause breakdowns

items.definition: Using devices for diagnosis, treatment, monitoring and admin in healthcare.
items.examTip: Must be highly reliable; patient data is very sensitive.
keyFacts: Scanners (MRI, CT) produce large image files, so hospitals need lots of fast storage
Patient monitors track vital signs, so staff are alerted at once if a patient's condition changes
Electronic records are shared by clinicians, so any doctor treating a patient sees their full history
Video GP appointments save patients travelling, so they suit people who are less mobile

items.definition: Using devices for design, music, video, animation and photography.
items.examTip: Creative work needs powerful hardware and lots of fast storage.
keyFacts: Need a powerful CPU, GPU and RAM, because editing video and 3D work is very demanding
Graphics tablets for drawing, so artists get precise, natural pen control
Large files (RAW, 4K video) need lots of storage and fast drives

items.definition: Machines and AI doing repetitive or complex tasks with little human input.
items.examples: Warehouse robots; car assembly lines; chatbots.
items.examTip: Efficiency vs job losses and retraining needs.
keyFacts: Works 24/7 with consistent quality, so output rises and mistakes fall
Takes on dangerous tasks, so workers are kept away from harm
Can replace jobs, especially repetitive manual work, which can increase unemployment
Needs new skills, so staff must be retrained to program and maintain the machines

subtopics.title: Forms of Notation for IT System Design

items.definition: Diagrams showing a system's components and how they connect.
items.examples: A network diagram of PCs, switch, router, server and internet.
items.examTip: Exam diagrams (6 marks): include every device from the scenario and label each connection type.
keyFacts: Show every device and connection, so anyone can see how the whole system fits together
Label connection types (Ethernet, Wi-Fi, 4G), so it is clear how data travels between devices
Use a cloud shape for the internet, which is the standard way to show it
Annotate what each part does, so the reader understands each part's role

items.definition: Diagrams showing the steps of a process using standard symbols.
items.examples: A login process checking a password.
items.examTip: Learn the symbols: oval start/end, rectangle process, diamond decision, parallelogram input/output.
keyFacts: Oval shows the start and end, so the reader knows where the process begins and finishes
Rectangle shows a process: an action or step that happens
Diamond shows a yes/no decision, with one arrow out for each answer
Parallelogram shows input or output, e.g. entering data or printing a receipt
Arrows show the flow, so the steps are followed in the right order

comparisonTable.title: System Diagram vs Flowchart
rows: Components of an IT system and their connections
Steps in a process or algorithm and their sequence
Logic, decisions, data flow through a process
Designing or documenting processes, algorithms, programs
Draw a network/system showing how components connect
Complete or draw a process showing steps and decisions

subtopics.title: Features and Uses of Peripheral Devices

items.definition: Hardware for getting data into a computer.
items.examples: Keyboard; mouse; microphone; barcode scanner; touchscreen.
items.examTip: Input = data going IN. Manual (keyboard) or automatic (sensor, scanner).
keyFacts: Manual input (keyboard, mouse, touchscreen) is controlled by a person, so it suits entering varied data
Optical input (scanner, barcode and QR readers, camera) reads data by light, so it is quick and accurate
Automatic input (sensors, RFID, biometrics) collects data with no human effort, so it can run 24/7

items.definition: Hardware that presents results from a computer to people.
items.examples: Monitor; printer; speakers; projector; braille display.
items.examTip: Output = data coming OUT. Printers make hard copy; screens make soft copy.
keyFacts: Visual output (monitor, printer, projector) shows results to read on screen or paper
Audio output (speakers, headphones) gives sound, e.g. alerts, music or screen-reader speech
Tactile output (braille display) lets blind users read by touch
Plotters produce large drawings, so they suit architects and engineers

items.definition: Hardware that keeps data so it can be used again later.
items.examples: Laptop SSD; external backup drive; USB stick.
items.examTip: Compare HDD and SSD on speed, cost and reliability.
keyFacts: HDD is a spinning disk that is cheap per GB, so it suits storing large amounts of data
SSD uses flash with no moving parts, so it is faster and less likely to break if dropped
USB sticks and external drives are portable, so they suit moving files between computers
NAS gives shared storage on a network, so a team can save to one place

items.definition: Keyboards adapted for users with physical, visual or learning difficulties.
items.examples: Large-key keyboards; one-handed keyboards.
items.examTip: For users who cannot use a standard keyboard.
keyFacts: Large keys help users with low vision or motor difficulties hit the right key
Key guards stop accidental presses, so users with tremors make fewer mistakes
One-handed layouts let users with the use of one hand type more quickly
On-screen keyboards can be used with a mouse, switch or eye tracker instead of physical keys

items.definition: Software that reads screen content aloud for blind or partially sighted users.
items.examples: JAWS; NVDA; VoiceOver.
items.examTip: Only works well if sites and apps are built accessibly.
keyFacts: Reads text, menus and buttons aloud, so blind users can use a computer independently
Used with the keyboard, not a mouse, because users can't see the pointer
Needs accessible design (WCAG), otherwise unlabelled buttons and images can't be read out

items.definition: A device that raises pins to form braille, so blind users can read the screen by touch.
items.examples: A refreshable braille display connected by USB.
items.examTip: Tactile output that updates as the screen changes.
keyFacts: Updates in real time as the user moves through the screen, so they can read as they go
Used with a screen reader, so the user can read by touch as well as listen
Expensive, so many blind users can't afford one without support

items.definition: Software that enlarges part or all of the screen for users with low vision.
items.examples: Windows Magnifier; zoom on macOS.
items.examTip: Makes things bigger, rather than reading them aloud.
keyFacts: Built into most operating systems, so users with low vision get it free without extra software
Typically 2× to 16× zoom, so the user can enlarge text and images as much as they need

items.definition: A stick or pointer worn on the head so users can press keys without using their hands.
items.examples: A head stick used by someone with paralysis.
items.examTip: For users with little or no arm or hand movement.
keyFacts: Presses keys or touchscreens, so users who can't use their hands can still type
Head-tracking cameras are the electronic version, moving the cursor as the head moves

items.definition: A single button that lets users with very limited movement control a computer.
items.examples: A large button switch; a cheek switch.
items.examTip: The computer cycles through options; the user presses to select.
keyFacts: Scanning highlights each option in turn, and the user presses the switch when the right one lights up
Any reliable movement can work the switch, e.g. a hand, chin or knee, so it suits very limited movement
Slow, but gives access to users who could not otherwise use a computer at all

items.definition: A pedal pressed by foot to trigger an action, keeping hands free.
items.examples: A pedal to pause audio while typing.
items.examTip: Assistive for users who can't use their hands, and a productivity tool.
keyFacts: One or several pedals, so different actions can be mapped to each foot press
Helps users with arm or hand impairments, because they can trigger actions with their feet

items.definition: A switch controlled by sucking or blowing into a tube.
items.examples: Controlling a wheelchair and computer by breath.
items.examTip: For users who can only reliably control their breathing.
keyFacts: Sip and puff act as different inputs, so the user can make choices using breath alone
Often used with scanning, so the user selects options as they are highlighted

items.definition: A camera that tracks where the user looks so they can control the cursor with their eyes.
items.examples: Tobii eye trackers for people with motor neurone disease.
items.examTip: Looking at a target for a moment (dwell) acts as a click.
keyFacts: Cursor follows your gaze, so looking at an item selects or points to it
Hands-free control, so it suits users with severe physical disabilities
Affected by lighting and glasses, which can make tracking less accurate

items.definition: Software that reads written text aloud as speech.
items.examples: Read Aloud in Word; communication apps for non-verbal users.
items.examTip: Helps people who can't read easily, and lets non-verbal users speak.
keyFacts: Helps with dyslexia and visual impairment, because users can listen instead of reading
Built into all major operating systems, so it is free and easy to turn on
AI voices sound increasingly natural, so listening for long periods is less tiring

subtopics.title: Characteristics and Implications of Storage Media

items.definition: How much data a storage medium can hold, measured in GB or TB.
items.examTip: Match capacity to the use: video editing needs TBs; documents need GBs.
keyFacts: USB sticks hold tens to hundreds of GB, so they suit moving documents and small media files
HDDs hold up to about 20 TB, so they suit large archives and backups
SSDs hold up to about 8 TB, so very large stores usually still use HDDs
HDDs are cheapest per GB, so they are chosen when lots of storage is needed on a budget

items.definition: The price of storage, especially the cost per gigabyte.
items.examTip: HDD is cheapest per GB; SSD costs more but is falling; cloud is an ongoing fee.
keyFacts: HDD is best for bulk storage, because it gives the most space for the money
SSD is worth it for the OS drive, because the computer starts and loads programs much faster
Cloud cost grows with usage, so it can become expensive as data builds up
Consider lifespan, not just price, because a cheap drive that fails early costs more overall

comparisonTable.title: Storage Media Compared: HDD vs SSD vs USB vs Optical
rows: Fragile — moving parts, vulnerable to drops

items.definition: How fast data is read from and written to storage.
items.examTip: Moving from HDD to SSD is the biggest speed upgrade for most computers.
keyFacts: HDD is slow because it has moving parts that must spin and seek to the data
SSD is several times faster, so programs open and files save much more quickly
NVMe SSD is fastest, because it connects directly to the motherboard's fast lanes
Optical discs are very slow, so they are now mainly used for archiving or distribution

items.definition: Whether the storage works with the device's connections, OS and hardware.
items.examTip: Check the connector, the file system and OS support.
keyFacts: Connectors (USB-A vs USB-C, SATA vs NVMe) must match, or the drive can't be plugged in
File systems (NTFS, APFS, exFAT) must be readable, or the OS can't open the files
Older devices may not support new drives, so upgrades can need adapters or new hardware

items.definition: Data entered and handled by people rather than computers.
items.examples: Writing appointments in a paper diary; counting stock by hand.
items.examTip: Slower and more error-prone, but flexible where judgement is needed.
keyFacts: More errors, because people make typing and copying mistakes
Slower, because each record is handled by hand
Humans can handle unusual cases that don't fit the rules a computer follows

items.definition: Data collected and processed by computers with little or no human input.
items.examples: EPOS updating stock at each sale; overnight bank processing.
items.examTip: Faster and more consistent. But a system error affects every record.
keyFacts: Faster with fewer errors, because computers process data without tiring or mistyping
Batch processing handles data together at set times, e.g. payroll run once a month
Real-time processing handles data immediately, e.g. booking a seat so it can't be sold twice
Data logging records sensor readings automatically, so data is collected 24/7 without staff

comparisonTable.title: Manual vs Automatic Data Processing
rows: Computer systems with minimal human input
Slow — limited by human working speed
Consistent — but systematic errors if algorithm is wrong
High initial setup; lower ongoing cost
Lower — may struggle with exceptions to normal rules
Can scale to process millions of transactions
Receptionist writing appointments in paper diary
EPOS system auto-updating stock when items are scanned

topics.title: Computer Software in an IT System

items.definition: An OS that processes groups of jobs automatically, without user interaction.
items.examples: Overnight bank payments; monthly payroll.
items.examTip: No interaction, runs in groups, often overnight. Results are not instant.
keyFacts: Efficient for large volumes, because jobs run together without waiting for a user
No real-time output, so results only appear when the whole batch has finished
Used in banking, payroll and billing, where the same job is done for thousands of records at once

items.definition: An OS that makes many separate computers work together as one system.
items.examples: Google spreading searches across thousands of servers.
items.examTip: Many computers acting as one: fault tolerant and scalable.
keyFacts: Spreads work across machines, so large tasks finish faster
One machine failing doesn't stop the system, because others take over its work
Add machines to grow, so capacity increases without replacing the system

items.definition: An OS that runs several programs at once by switching the CPU between them quickly.
items.examples: Browsing while music plays and a file downloads.
items.examTip: The CPU switches so fast it seems simultaneous.
keyFacts: Switches rapidly between processes, so several programs appear to run at the same time
Needs enough RAM for all open programs, otherwise the computer slows down
Most modern OSs multitask, so users can e.g. browse while music plays

items.definition: An OS on a server that manages shared files, printers and user accounts for a network.
items.examples: Windows Server.
items.examTip: Runs on servers; clients connect for files, printers and logins.
keyFacts: Central user accounts and logins, so staff can log in from any computer on the network
Shares files and printers, so resources don't need to be duplicated on every machine
Handles many clients at once, so a whole organisation can use the network together

items.definition: An OS that must respond to inputs within a guaranteed, very short time.
items.examples: ABS brakes; aircraft controls; a pacemaker.
items.examTip: About being predictable, not just fast. Used where delay is dangerous.
keyFacts: Guaranteed response time, so the system reacts instantly when a delay could be dangerous
Used in medical, transport and industrial systems, e.g. pacemakers and car airbags
Reliability over features, because a crash or slow response could cost lives

items.definition: An OS designed for phones, tablets and wearables.
items.examples: iOS; Android.
items.examTip: Built for touch, battery life and apps from app stores.
keyFacts: Touch-first interface, so it is easy to use on a small screen without a keyboard
Manages battery and sensors, so the device lasts all day
Apps run separately (sandboxed) for security, so one bad app can't access another's data
App-store distribution, so apps are checked before users can install them

items.definition: A stripped-down OS that does one job only.
items.examples: An ATM; a self-service kiosk.
items.examTip: Reliable and secure, but can't be used for anything else.
keyFacts: One function only, e.g. a smart TV or cash machine, so it is simple and reliable
Fewer vulnerabilities, because there is less software for attackers to exploit
Can't run other software, so it can't be repurposed if needs change

items.definition: An OS that lets several users use the same system at once, each with their own account.
items.examples: A Linux server with many remote users.
items.examTip: Must keep each user's files and sessions separate.
keyFacts: Each user has a private session, so their files and settings are kept separate
Login required, so the system knows who each user is and what they may access
The OS shares resources between users, so one user can't hog the CPU or memory

comparisonTable.title: Operating System Types Compared
rows: Processes jobs in groups without user interaction
Multiple programs appear to run simultaneously
Office server managing files and users
Multiple simultaneous users with isolated sessions

subtopics.title: Role of the Operating System in Managing

items.definition: The OS handles network protocols, connections, sending and receiving data, and bandwidth.
items.examTip: Four parts: protocols, connections, transmission, resource monitoring.
keyFacts: Runs protocols such as TCP/IP, so the computer can communicate with any other device on the network
Sets up and ends connections, so data reaches the right program on the right device
Splits data into packets and reassembles them, so large files can travel across the network reliably
Assigns IP settings (e.g. via DHCP), so devices join the network without manual set-up

items.definition: The OS protects the system through access control, malware protection, encryption and a firewall.
items.examTip: Know the four areas and what each does.
keyFacts: Access control through logins and permissions, so users only reach what they're allowed to
Malware protection (e.g. Windows Defender) is built in, so the device is protected without extra software
Drive encryption (e.g. BitLocker), so data on a lost or stolen device can't be read
Built-in firewall blocks unwanted network traffic, protecting the device on any network

items.definition: The OS gives RAM to programs, keeps them apart, and uses virtual memory when RAM runs out.
items.examTip: Name the parts: allocation, protection, virtual memory, swapping and paging.
keyFacts: Allocates RAM when a program starts and frees it when it ends, so memory isn't wasted
Programs can't touch each other's memory, so one crashing program doesn't bring down the others
Virtual memory uses disk as extra RAM, so more programs can run, but it is slower
Paging swaps small blocks between RAM and disk, so only the parts in use need to be in RAM

items.definition: The OS shares CPU time between running programs by scheduling and switching between them.
items.examTip: Name the parts: scheduling, CPU time management, context switching.
keyFacts: Scheduling decides which process runs next, so the CPU is shared fairly
Round robin gives equal time slices in turn, so no program is left waiting forever
Priority lets important tasks go first, so urgent work isn't held up
Context switching saves and restores each process, so it carries on exactly where it stopped

items.definition: Software that lets the OS talk to a hardware device.
items.examTip: Without the right driver, the OS can't use the device.
keyFacts: Translates OS commands for the device, so the OS doesn't need to know how every device works
Reports device errors back to the OS, so problems like a paper jam can be shown to the user
Outdated drivers cause crashes and security holes, so they should be kept up to date
items.examples: A printer driver; a graphics card driver.

items.definition: The OS checks who users are, stores their settings, and lets admins manage accounts.
items.examTip: Name the parts: authentication, profiles, account management tools.
keyFacts: Log in with a password, PIN, biometric or MFA, so the OS knows who is using the computer
Each user has their own profile and files, so people sharing a computer keep their work private
Account types (administrator, standard, guest) limit what each user can change, protecting the system

subtopics.title: Types, Uses and Features of Software

items.definition: Software that maintains and looks after the computer system.
items.examples: Antivirus; backup; disk defragmenter; file compression.
items.examTip: Utility software maintains the system. It is not application software.
keyFacts: Antivirus removes malware, keeping the computer and its data safe
Defragmenter speeds up HDDs by putting each file's pieces back together (SSDs don't need it)
Backup software automates copies, so backups happen even if people forget
Compression shrinks files, so they take up less storage and send faster

items.definition: Software people use to do tasks and create things.
items.examples: Word; Excel; Photoshop; a web browser.
items.examTip: Application software is for doing work, not maintaining the system.
keyFacts: Word processors, spreadsheets and databases let users create documents, do calculations and store records
Browsers and email let users find information and communicate
Can be general or specialist (e.g. CAD), with specialist software built for one job

subtopics.title: Factors Impacting Choice of OS and Application Software

items.definition: The cost of buying, licensing and running software.
items.examTip: Open source is often free; proprietary has licence fees but vendor support.
keyFacts: One-off licence vs subscription: a licence costs more up front, a subscription costs more over time
Free alternatives (e.g. LibreOffice) cut licence costs, though they may lack some features
Hidden costs such as training and migration can make cheap software expensive overall

items.definition: How well software protects data, including how often it gets security updates.
items.examTip: Especially important when choosing an OS.
keyFacts: Patches must be installed promptly, because attackers target known flaws
Windows is targeted most because it's most used, so attackers get the most victims
Open-source code can be checked by anyone, so flaws may be found and fixed quickly

items.definition: Whether software works with the hardware and other software already in use.
items.examTip: Incompatible software is useless however good it is.
keyFacts: Must meet the minimum hardware requirements, or it will run slowly or not at all
Drivers must exist for existing printers and devices, or that hardware stops working
Must open existing file formats, so old documents and data can still be used

items.definition: Whether the software has the functions the organisation needs.
items.examTip: Features must match the job; extras add cost and complexity.
keyFacts: Must meet specific requirements, otherwise staff can't do their jobs with it
Specialist tools may only be proprietary, so organisations may have to pay for them

items.definition: Whether the software fits the organisation's tasks and its users' skills.
items.examTip: Start here in scenarios: what must it do, and who will use it?
keyFacts: Must do every required task, or staff will need extra software or workarounds
Interface should suit users' skills, so staff can use it without lots of training
Industry-standard software may be needed, so files can be shared with clients and partners

items.definition: How well the software runs on the available hardware.
items.examTip: Heavy software on weak hardware = slow and unproductive.
keyFacts: Quick response to input, so staff aren't kept waiting
Doesn't hog RAM or CPU, so other programs keep running smoothly
Stable under heavy use, so it doesn't crash and lose work at busy times

items.definition: A text interface where the user types commands.
items.examples: Command Prompt; Linux Terminal.
items.examTip: Fast and powerful for experts, but commands must be memorised.
keyFacts: No mouse needed, so commands can be typed quickly by experienced users
Tasks can be scripted, so repetitive jobs are automated and run the same way each time
Uses few resources, so it suits servers and older hardware
Hard for beginners, because commands must be remembered and typed exactly

items.definition: An interface where users choose from a list of options.
items.examples: ATM screens; "press 1 for sales" phone menus.
items.examTip: Simple and guided, but limited to the options shown.
keyFacts: No prior knowledge needed, because users just pick from the options shown
Can't do anything not on the menu, so it is limited but hard to get wrong
Slow for experts, because they must go through several menus to reach an option

items.definition: A visual interface with windows, icons, menus and a pointer (WIMP).
items.examples: The Windows desktop; macOS.
items.examTip: Easiest for non-technical users, but uses more resources than a CLI.
keyFacts: Windows, Icons, Menus, Pointer (WIMP) let users point and click instead of typing commands
Intuitive visual design, so new users learn it quickly
Needs more processing power, because it must draw graphics on screen
Slower than CLI for repetitive tasks, because each step needs clicking through

items.definition: A GUI controlled by touch gestures instead of a mouse.
items.examples: Smartphones; self-checkouts.
items.examTip: Needs bigger buttons; ideal for phones and kiosks.
keyFacts: Tap, swipe and pinch gestures are natural, so even young children can use it
Larger touch targets, because fingers are less precise than a mouse pointer
Used on phones, tablets and kiosks, where there is no room for a keyboard or mouse

subtopics.title: Principles and Implications of Open Source and Proprietary Software

items.term: Open Source vs Proprietary Operating Systems
items.definition: Open-source OS code is free to view and change (Linux); proprietary code is closed (Windows, macOS).
items.examples: Linux vs Windows; Android vs iOS.
items.examTip: Give advantages AND disadvantages of both.
keyFacts: Open source is free, customisable and community-supported, so organisations save on licences
Open source can be less polished with patchy driver support, so some hardware may not work
Proprietary is consistent with vendor support, so problems are fixed by the company
Proprietary has licence costs and locks you to one vendor, making switching expensive

comparisonTable.title: Open Source vs Proprietary Software
rows: Publicly available — can be viewed, modified, redistributed
Closed — only vendor can access and modify
Community forums, documentation, optional paid support
Vendor provides dedicated support (often included or paid)
Many eyes on the code — bugs found quickly; also visible to attackers
Vendor controls patches; smaller attack surface visibility; faster coordinated response
Highly customisable — modify code for specific needs
Limited customisation — only features vendor provides
May have driver/compatibility issues with some hardware or proprietary formats
Designed to work with mainstream hardware; vendor-controlled ecosystem
Low — can switch, fork, or modify freely

items.term: Open Source vs Proprietary Application Software
items.definition: The same open-source vs proprietary choice, applied to applications.
items.examples: LibreOffice vs Microsoft 365; GIMP vs Photoshop.
items.examTip: Also consider file compatibility: proprietary formats may not open correctly.
keyFacts: Free alternatives may lack advanced features, so power users may still need paid software
Some industries require specific proprietary tools, so files can be shared with clients
Saving licence fees can cost more in support, because staff need training and help

subtopics.title: Features of Common File Types and Formats

items.definition: Image formats differ in compression, quality and features.
items.examples: JPEG photos; PNG logos; SVG icons.
items.examTip: JPEG lossy (photos); PNG lossless (transparency); SVG scalable; RAW largest.
keyFacts: JPEG is lossy and small, so it suits photos on websites
PNG is lossless with transparency, so it suits logos and screenshots
GIF has 256 colours and animation, so it suits simple animated images
SVG scales without losing quality, because it stores shapes, not pixels, so it suits icons and logos

items.definition: Audio formats differ in compression, size and quality.
items.examples: MP3 streaming; WAV recording.
items.examTip: MP3/AAC for streaming; WAV/FLAC for production. Higher bit rate = better and bigger.
keyFacts: MP3 is lossy and small, so it suits music on phones and streaming
AAC is lossy but sounds better than MP3 at the same size, so many streaming services use it
WAV is uncompressed, so it keeps full quality for editing but files are large
FLAC is lossless but smaller than WAV, so it suits storing music at full quality

items.definition: A video file is a container (e.g. MP4) holding streams compressed by a codec.
items.examples: MP4 online; MOV from Apple devices.
items.examTip: H.265 is half the size of H.264 at the same quality.
keyFacts: MP4 with H.264 is the most compatible, so it plays almost everywhere
MP4 with H.265 is smaller at the same quality, so it suits 4K video
MKV holds several audio and subtitle tracks, so it suits films in more than one language

items.definition: Installer and program formats specific to each operating system.
items.examples: EXE/MSI on Windows; DMG on macOS; APK on Android.
items.examTip: Only install from trusted sources and check digital signatures.
keyFacts: EXE runs programs and MSI installs them on Windows, so they won't run on other OSs
APK installs Android apps, usually from the Play Store
DMG installs macOS apps, so it is used only on Macs
ZIP must be extracted first, because it is a compressed folder, not a program

subtopics.title: Factors Affecting the Choice of IT Systems

items.definition: What the people using the system need: their tasks, skills, mobility and accessibility needs.
items.examTip: Always start with user needs: who will use it and what for?
keyFacts: Identify the users first, because the right system depends on who will use it
Skill level shapes the interface, so beginners get a simpler design and experts more control
Accessibility needs must be met, so disabled users aren't excluded
Mobile or fixed? Decides whether laptops and tablets or desktops are needed

items.definition: The technical requirements the system must meet, e.g. performance, storage and ports.
keyFacts: Sets minimum performance, so the system can handle the workload
Based on real needs, so money isn't wasted on power nobody uses
Used to compare options fairly, by checking each against the same requirements

items.definition: Whether the system works with existing hardware, software, data and networks.
keyFacts: Works with existing devices and software, so nothing already owned has to be replaced
Existing data can be moved across, so records aren't lost or re-typed
Suits the current network, so no expensive network upgrade is needed

items.definition: The network and device connections the system supports.
keyFacts: Ethernet, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth support, so it connects to the network and nearby devices
Ports must match peripherals (USB, HDMI), so existing screens and devices can be plugged in
4G/5G for use on the move, so staff can work away from Wi-Fi
Supports VPN or remote access, so staff can reach internal systems securely from outside

items.definition: The total cost of buying, setting up, running and replacing the system.
items.examTip: Consider total cost of ownership, not just the purchase price.
keyFacts: Upfront purchase or lease: buying costs more at the start, leasing spreads the cost
Running costs (support, licences, power) continue for the system's whole life
Training costs, because staff need time to learn the new system
Is it worth the money? The benefits must outweigh the total cost

items.definition: How well the system uses time, money and resources to do its job.
keyFacts: Lower energy use cuts costs, especially when systems run all day
Faster processing saves time, so staff get more done
Automates manual steps, so fewer staff hours are needed

items.definition: Practicalities of rollout: timescales, testing, moving data and downtime.
items.examTip: Cover all four: timescales, testing, migration, downtime.
keyFacts: Rollout can take weeks or months, so it must be planned around busy periods
Test with real users before go-live, so problems are found before they disrupt work
Moving data risks loss or corruption, so it must be backed up and checked
Phased rollout or running old and new side by side reduces risk, because the old system is a fallback

items.definition: How the system affects how much work staff can get done.
keyFacts: Short dip while staff learn, because they are slower at first
Long-term gains once adopted, as staff become faster than with the old system
Automates manual tasks, freeing staff for more valuable work

items.definition: The security features of the system and how it fits existing security measures.
keyFacts: Regular updates from the vendor, so new security flaws are patched
Supports MFA, so a stolen password alone can't get into accounts
Meets standards and GDPR, so the organisation stays within the law

items.definition: Systems that track stock in real time and reorder automatically when it runs low.
items.examples: Supermarket tills reducing stock counts at each sale.
items.examTip: Benefits: fewer stockouts, less overstock. Risk: if it fails, stock levels are unknown.
keyFacts: Barcodes/RFID update stock at the till, so stock levels are always accurate
Low stock triggers reorders, so shelves are never empty
Less manual counting, which saves staff time and cuts errors
Managers see stock from anywhere, so they can make decisions without visiting each shop

items.definition: Sensors or systems automatically recording time-stamped readings over time.
items.examples: A weather station; factory temperature sensors.
items.examTip: Automatic, continuous and time-stamped. Link to IoT sensors.
keyFacts: No human needed, so data is collected 24/7, even in dangerous or remote places
Each reading is time-stamped, so changes can be tracked over time
Produces large amounts of data, so storage and analysis tools are needed
Analysed later for trends, e.g. finding when a machine tends to overheat

items.definition: Using IT to find patterns and trends in data to guide decisions.
items.examples: Choosing which products to promote from sales data; spotting fraud.
items.examTip: Turns raw data into decisions.
keyFacts: Dashboards and reports show key figures clearly, so managers see problems quickly
Forecasts from past data predict future demand, so stock and staff can be planned
Decisions based on evidence, not guesswork, so they are more likely to succeed

items.definition: IT for everyday admin: documents, spreadsheets, email and scheduling.
items.examples: Microsoft 365; Teams; Zoom.
keyFacts: Office suites are standard, so staff already know them and files are easy to share
Cloud versions allow collaboration, so several people can edit a document at once
Document systems control versions, so everyone works on the latest copy

items.definition: IT for design, media production and animation.
items.examples: Photoshop; AutoCAD; Blender.
keyFacts: Needs powerful hardware, because editing video and 3D models is demanding
Large files need fast, big storage, so work loads and saves quickly
Often subscription software (e.g. Adobe), so costs continue every month

items.definition: IT for creating, targeting and measuring adverts.
items.examples: Google Ads; Facebook ad targeting.
keyFacts: Targeted using personal data, so adverts reach the people most likely to buy
Results measured in real time, so poorly performing adverts can be changed quickly
Links to targeted marketing and ethics, because using personal data raises privacy concerns

items.definition: IT that designs, controls and checks manufacturing, from CAD to quality control.
items.examples: CAD designs sent to CNC machines.
keyFacts: CAD is used to design products on screen, so changes are quick and cheap to make
CAM turns designs into machine instructions, so there is no manual programming step
CNC gives precise automated machining, so every part comes out identical
Sensors spot defects, so faulty products are caught before they reach customers

items.definition: IT for physical and cyber security, e.g. CCTV and access control.
items.examples: Networked CCTV; biometric locks on a server room.
keyFacts: CCTV with remote viewing, so sites can be watched from anywhere
Swipe cards and biometrics control who enters, and log every entry
Security monitoring software spots attacks on the network quickly
Creates lots of data to store, e.g. CCTV footage and access logs

items.definition: IT performing tasks with little or no human input.
items.examples: Automated payroll; chatbots; robot arms.
keyFacts: Cuts labour costs, because machines do work people used to be paid for
Consistent every time, so quality doesn't drop with tiredness
Can replace jobs, especially repetitive roles, which affects staff and the local community

subtopics.title: Impact and Implications of IT Systems on Organisations

items.term: User Experience (Ease of Use, Performance, Availability, Accessibility)
items.definition: How easy, fast, available and accessible a system is for staff and customers.
items.examTip: Cover all four: ease of use, performance, availability, accessibility.
keyFacts: Easy to use means fewer errors and less training, so staff are productive sooner
Slow systems cut productivity, because staff spend time waiting
Downtime costs sales, because customers can't buy while the system is down
Usable by people with disabilities, so no staff or customers are excluded

items.definition: Whether the system meets the needs of both staff and customers.
keyFacts: Staff need the right features without extra work, or they'll find workarounds
Customers need reliable, easy systems, or they'll go to a competitor
Collect feedback to improve, so problems are found and fixed

items.definition: The cost of the system to the organisation, now and over time.
keyFacts: Upfront costs: hardware, licences and installation, paid before any benefit is seen
Ongoing costs: support, maintenance and training, which continue for years
Hidden costs such as data migration and integration are often underestimated

items.definition: How the rollout affects the organisation: timescales, testing, data migration and downtime.
items.examTip: Focus on the impact during and after rollout.
keyFacts: Rushed rollouts cause problems, because bugs and training gaps aren't dealt with first
Test with real users, so problems are found before go-live
Data can be lost when moving it, so it must be backed up first
Downtime stops normal work, so switch-over should happen at quiet times

items.term: Replacement or Integration with Current Systems
items.definition: Whether the new system replaces the old one entirely or works alongside it.
items.examTip: Replace: clean break but risky and costly. Integrate: lower risk but more complex.
keyFacts: Full replacement has higher risk and cost, because everything changes at once
Integration works alongside the old system but is more complex to set up and maintain
APIs let systems share data, so old and new systems can work together

items.definition: How the system affects staff output during and after the change.
keyFacts: Dip while staff learn, because they are slower with an unfamiliar system
Long-term gains once staff are confident with it
Automation frees staff for other work, such as customer service

items.definition: How the system changes the way staff work.
keyFacts: Enables remote and flexible working, so staff can work from home
Messaging replaces some email, so communication is quicker and less formal
Some roles change or disappear, as tasks are automated
Staff may resist change, so managers need to explain the benefits and involve them

items.definition: Training staff need to use the system, at launch and as it changes.
items.examTip: Training costs time and money, but too little leads to errors and poor adoption.
keyFacts: Train everyone before go-live, so staff can use the system from day one
Refresher training after updates, so staff keep up with new features
Different users need different training, e.g. admins need more than everyday users

items.definition: Ongoing help for staff using the system.
keyFacts: Internal IT helpdesk, so staff get quick help from people who know the organisation
Vendor support contracts, so complex problems are fixed by the experts who made the system
FAQs and guides reduce helpdesk load, because staff can solve simple problems themselves

items.definition: The new security risks a system brings and how it must be protected.
keyFacts: Every new system adds vulnerabilities, so it increases the ways attackers could get in
Change insecure default settings, because attackers know common default passwords
Keep it patched, so known security flaws are fixed
Set permissions carefully from day one, so staff only access what they need

items.term: How Emerging Technologies and AI Affect IT System Performance
items.definition: AI and new technologies such as 5G and edge computing make systems faster and more capable.
items.examples: AI chips in phones; 5G for real-time applications.
items.examTip: Performance gains, but they need new infrastructure and lots of computing power.
keyFacts: AI chips run AI tasks much faster, so features like voice recognition work on the device itself
Edge computing processes data near its source, cutting delay because it doesn't travel to a far-off server
5G is very fast with very low latency, so it suits live video and self-driving cars
AI tunes systems by learning from use, e.g. adjusting performance to save battery

items.term: Implications of Emerging Technologies and AI on Personal Use of IT Systems
items.definition: How AI changes everyday personal use, from voice assistants to AI-generated content.
items.examples: Siri and Alexa; Netflix recommendations; deepfakes.
items.examTip: Give both sides: convenience and accessibility vs privacy, misinformation and over-reliance.
keyFacts: Voice assistants help accessibility, so people with disabilities can control devices by speaking
Personalised recommendations save time, but can trap users in filter bubbles
Deepfakes spread misinformation, because fake video and audio look and sound real
Needs lots of personal data, which raises privacy concerns about how it is used and stored

items.term: Implications of Emerging Technologies and AI on Organisations
items.definition: How AI and emerging technology change the way organisations operate and employ people.
items.examples: AI fraud detection in banks; AI screening job applications.
items.examTip: Both sides for Level 3: efficiency and better decisions vs job losses, bias and security.
keyFacts: Automates tasks that needed people, so organisations cut costs and work faster
Better, faster decisions from data, because AI spots patterns humans miss
Jobs lost, including office roles, so staff may need retraining
Bias in training data leads to unfair decisions, and attackers use AI too, e.g. for convincing phishing
